facts.claim: Mac DeMarco and Italian singer Ryan Paris (real name Fabio Roscioli) are credited as the songwriters of 'Simply Paradise'. Publishing is registered through SOCAN for DeMarco and GEMA for Paris.
The single came out on 2 October 2023 on Mac's Record Label and runs 2:36.
The collaboration began with DeMarco's 2014 Pitchfork documentary 'Pepperoni Playboy'. In it he praised Paris's 1983 hit 'Dolce Vita' as an inspiration and danced down the street to it.
Paris saw the video and invited DeMarco to do a remix of 'Dolce Vita' together. DeMarco replied in a 2016 video that he was interested, and the pair did not work together until 2023.
Instead of a 'Dolce Vita' remix, the pair made a new original song.
DeMarco said Paris invited him in September 2023 to his home by the beach outside Rome. He said the song and video came out of the three nights he spent there.

Paris said they had agreed in advance to write a song together. He said they got the idea of doing it like Michael Jackson and Paul McCartney's 'The Girl Is Mine' and finished the song in a few hours.
The music video was shot by DeMarco's longtime partner, Kiera McNally.
The Fader described the song as bittersweet, crushed-velvet R&B in which the two singers trade lines in the manner of 'The Girl Is Mine'. The video was filmed at sunset on an Italian beach.
Paris and DeMarco performed 'Simply Paradise' and 'Dolce Vita' together at several stops of DeMarco's European tour. A later collaboration, 'Still What I'm Looking For', followed the single.

research.lineage: A mellow, guitar-led R&B and soft-rock duet that grew from DeMarco's fandom for Ryan Paris's 1983 Italo-disco hit 'Dolce Vita' and is modeled on the Michael Jackson and Paul McCartney duet 'The Girl Is Mine'.

draft:
Near the end of **Simply Paradise**, the song stops pretending to be a song and turns into two guys talking. "But listen, Mac," someone says, and then the clincher: "'Italian do it better', Madonna said." The reply comes back half-convinced: "Madonna? Sure, she knows." It's a throwaway, and it's the best moment on the record, because it gives away what the whole thing is really about. This is a love song about a woman neither singer seems to know, sung by two men who clearly like each other a lot.

The setup is borrowed on purpose. Ryan Paris has said he and Mac DeMarco took their idea from Michael Jackson and Paul McCartney's "The Girl Is Mine," and they keep that duet's frame: two voices trading lines and claiming the same woman. The boasts are cartoonish. "Don't try, don't try to have her," one warns. The other gets told "your love is ordinary," the kind of insult you only throw at a friend. That's the emotional trick. Every line is possessive, but the feeling underneath is warmth, maybe even gratitude. The rivalry is just the excuse to stand at the same mic.

The backstory makes that warmth easy to believe. In his 2014 Pitchfork documentary *Pepperoni Playboy*, DeMarco called Paris's 1983 Italo-disco hit "Dolce Vita" an inspiration and danced down the street to it. Paris saw the video and offered to remix the song with him. DeMarco said yes in a 2016 video, and then nothing happened for seven years. In September 2023, Paris invited him to his home by the beach outside Rome. They wrote this in a few hours, and the song and its video came out of three nights there. Kiera McNally, DeMarco's longtime partner, shot the clip at sunset. Under the swagger, you can hear a fan who finally got the call.

It doesn't sound like "Dolce Vita," though. Where you might expect Italo-disco gloss, the band lopes along instead. A clean electric guitar picks out arpeggiated chords, the bass walks a simple line, and the drums swing easy at a moderate tempo, with the snare pushed forward. The vocal is clear and mid-range, smooth and in no hurry, with a little reverb around it, and the production stays polished. The Fader called it bittersweet, crushed-velvet R&B, and that fits. Nothing in the groove is fighting over anybody.

The lyrics are thin, and some lines barely make sense ("I know I can make you turn bad"). The song doesn't hide that. It's built from "yeah-yeah" and the two-word title, and that loose, half-finished quality is part of the charm.

What sticks is the gap between what the song says and what it means: two men insist the girl is theirs, and you end up hearing a long-delayed friendship finally getting its turn.
